questions.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨t,\,{e}^{t},\,{e}^{-t}⟩$ at the point where $t=0,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
questions.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=0$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(0)$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

 

$$
R(u)=r(0)+u{r}^{′}(0),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,\,{e}^{0},\,{e}^{-0}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,{e}^{t},\,-{e}^{-t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0) & =⟨1,\,{e}^{0},\,-{e}^{-0}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point 
 where $t=0$ is

$$
R(u)=⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩+u⟨1,\,1,\,-1⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨-\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3},2t-1⟩,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨-1,-1⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2{t}^{2},2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $⟨-1,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨-1,-1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨-1,-1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨-1,-1⟩\cdot ⟨-2{t}^{2},2⟩ & =0 \\ (-1)(-2{t}^{2})+(-1)(2) & =0 \\ 2{t}^{2}-2 & =0 \\ 2(t+1)(t-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $t=\pm 1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨-\frac{2(-1)^{3}}{3},2(-1)-1⟩=⟨\frac{2}{3},-3⟩, \\ r(1) & =⟨-\frac{2(1)^{3}}{3},2(1)-1⟩=⟨-\frac{2}{3},1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨-1,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the points $(-\frac{2}{3},1)$ and $(\frac{2}{3},-3).$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+1\,,\,2t-1⟩,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨1\,,\,-2⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t\,,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $⟨1\,,\,-2⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨1\,,\,-2⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨1\,,\,-2⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨1\,,\,-2⟩\cdot ⟨2t\,,\,2⟩ & =0 \\ 1\cdot 2t+(-2)\cdot 2 & =0 \\ 2t-4 & =0 \\ 2(t-2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=2.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨{(2)}^{2}+1\,,\,2(2)-1⟩=⟨5\,,\,3⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1\,,\,-2⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(5,3).$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{4}+4t\,,\,{t}^{3}-2t\,,\,2{t}^{3}-3t⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4}+4t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-3t)⟩ \\  & =⟨4{t}^{3}+4,\,3{t}^{2}-2,\,6{t}^{2}-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩ \\ ⟨4{t}^{3}+4,\,3{t}^{2}-2,\,6{t}^{2}-3⟩ & =c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩ \\ ⟨4{t}^{3}+4,\,3{t}^{2}-2,\,6{t}^{2}-3⟩ & =⟨0\,,\,c\,,\,3c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4{t}^{3}+4=0 \\ 3{t}^{2}-2=c \\ 6{t}^{2}-3=3c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $t=-1.$ Substituting to the second equation, we get $c=1.$
These values also satisfy the third equation. 

Therefore, $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨(-1)^{4}+4(-1)\,,\,(-1)^{3}-2(-1)\,,\,2(-1)^{3}-3(-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,\,1,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(-3,1,1).$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\sqrt{t}\,,\,{t}^{3}+5\,,\,2t+2⟩,$ $t\in (0,\infty ),$ find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+5),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+2)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},\,3{t}^{2},\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ ⟨\sqrt{t},\,{t}^{3}+5,\,2t+2⟩ & =c\,⟨\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},\,3{t}^{2},\,2⟩ \\ ⟨\sqrt{t},\,{t}^{3}+5,\,2t+2⟩ & =⟨\frac{c}{2\sqrt{t}},\,3c{t}^{2},\,2c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{t}=\frac{c}{2\sqrt{t}} \\ {t}^{3}+5=3c{t}^{2} \\ 2t+2=2c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=2t.$ Substituting into the third equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2t+2 & =2\cdot (2t) \\ 2t+2 & =4t \\ 2t-2 & =0 \\ t & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This satisfies also the second equation ${t}^{3}+5=3c{t}^{2}.$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1.$ These values also satisfy the second equation. 

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨\sqrt{1}\,,\,{1}^{3}+5\,,\,2(1)+2⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,6,\,4⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,6,4).$
